title: Methods
description: Learn how to define and use methods in C#.

data.text: Methods are the fundamental building blocks of C# programs. They let you encapsulate reusable logic, organize your code into meaningful units, and make your programs easier to read, test, and maintain. In this lesson, you'll learn how to define methods with parameters and return types, use method overloading, and apply advanced parameter modifiers like `ref`, `out`, and `in`.
What is a Method?

A method is a named block of code that performs a specific task. You define a method once, then call (invoke) it whenever you need that task performed. Methods can accept input values called **parameters** and can optionally **return** a result.
Method Anatomy

data.title: Parts of a Method Declaration
items: **Access modifier** (e.g., `public`, `private`) — Who can call this method
**Return type** (e.g., `int`, `string`, `void`) — What type of value the method gives back
**Method name** (e.g., `CalculateTotal`) — What you call to invoke it
**Parameters** (e.g., `(int a, int b)`) — Input values the method needs
**Method body** (`{ ... }`) — The code that runs when the method is called

data.content: A simple method that adds two numbers

data.text: Return Types

The return type tells the compiler what kind of value a method will produce. If a method does not produce a value, use `void`. Otherwise, specify the type of value returned. The `return` keyword sends a value back to the caller and immediately exits the method.

data.title: Different Return Types
Void vs Return
data.text: A `void` method cannot use `return value;` — it can only use `return;` to exit early. Attempting to return a value from a void method is a compile-time error.
Parameters
Parameters let you pass data into a method. When you call a method, you provide **arguments** that are assigned to the method's parameters. C# offers several parameter types for different scenarios.
Required vs Optional Parameters
By default, all parameters are **required** — you must provide a value when calling the method. You can make parameters **optional** by assigning them a default value in the method signature.

data.title: Optional Parameters
Named Arguments
data.text: Named arguments let you specify parameters by name instead of position, making calls more readable and allowing you to skip optional parameters. Use `loudly: true` instead of providing every preceding parameter.
The params Array
The `params` keyword allows a method to accept a variable number of arguments. The compiler creates an array from the arguments, so you can pass as many values as needed.

data.title: Using params for Variable Arguments
data.content: A method that accepts any number of integers

data.title: params Rules
data.text: A method can have only one `params` parameter, and it must be the last parameter. You can pass individual values or an array — the compiler handles both.
Method Overloading

**Method overloading** allows you to define multiple methods with the same name but different parameter lists. The compiler selects the appropriate method based on the number and types of arguments passed. This provides flexibility and a consistent API.

data.title: Method Overloading
data.content: Multiple Print methods with different parameter signatures

data.text: Resolution Rules

The compiler resolves overloaded methods at compile time based on: (1) the number of arguments, (2) the types of arguments, and (3) the presence of optional parameters. If no exact match is found, the compiler attempts implicit conversions.

data.title: Ambiguous Overloads
data.text: Avoid overloads that could cause ambiguity. For example, having both `Print(int)` and `Print(double)` can be confusing when called with `Print(5)` — the compiler prefers `int`, but adding `Print(long)` could create ambiguity.
ref, out, and in Parameters

By default, C# passes arguments **by value**, meaning the method receives a copy of the value. For reference types, this means a copy of the reference (the object itself is shared). The `ref`, `out`, and `in` keywords let you pass arguments **by reference**, giving the method direct access to the original variable.

cards.title: ref
cards.description: Passes a variable by reference. The method can read and modify the original variable. The variable must be initialized before calling.
pros: Variable must be initialized before call
cons: Can make code harder to follow

cards.title: out
cards.description: Passes a variable by reference specifically for returning multiple values. The method MUST assign a value before returning. Variable does NOT need initialization.
pros: Return multiple values from a method
cons: Method is forced to assign a value

cards.title: in
cards.description: Passes a variable by reference for read-only access. The method can read but NOT modify the original variable. Useful for large structs to avoid copying.

data.title: ref, out, and in Examples
data.content: Demonstrating all three parameter passing modes

data.title: out Requires Assignment
data.text: A method with an `out` parameter MUST assign a value to that parameter on every possible execution path before returning. The compiler enforces this — you will get a compile error if you forget.
Recursion

**Recursion** is when a method calls itself to solve a smaller instance of the same problem. Every recursive method needs: (1) a **base case** that stops the recursion, and (2) a **recursive case** that breaks the problem into a smaller one.

data.title: Recursive Factorial
Stack Overflow
data.text: Every recursive call adds a frame to the call stack. Deep recursion (e.g., Factorial(10000)) can cause a StackOverflowException. For very deep recursion, use iteration or `System.Runtime.CompilerServices.MethodImplOptions.AggressiveInlining` carefully.
Expression-Bodied Members

Expression-bodied members let you write concise method definitions using the `=>` (lambda) syntax when the method body is a single expression. This reduces boilerplate and improves readability for simple methods.

data.title: Expression-Bodied Methods and Properties
data.content: Writing concise methods with the => syntax

data.title: When to Use Expression Bodies
data.text: Expression-bodied members are ideal for simple getters, calculations, and conversions. Avoid them for complex logic with multiple statements — use a full method body for readability.
Local Functions

**Local functions** are methods defined inside another method. They are useful for helper logic that is only relevant within the containing method. Local functions can access variables from the enclosing scope (closures) and can use `async`/`await`.

data.title: Local Functions
data.content: Using local functions for helper logic

data.title: Local Functions vs Lambdas
data.text: Local functions are more powerful than lambdas: they support generics, can have access modifiers, support `ref`/`out` parameters, and have better stack trace readability. Use local functions for complex helpers; use lambdas for short, inline delegates.
Method Overloading vs Default Parameters
Both method overloading and optional parameters with default values can achieve similar results. Choosing between them depends on your API design preferences.

cards.title: Method Overloading
cards.description: Define multiple methods with the same name but different parameter signatures.
pros: Clear intent — each method has a distinct signature
No risk of breaking changes when adding new overloads
cons: Can lead to many similar method definitions

cards.title: Optional Parameters
cards.description: Define a single method with parameters that have default values.
pros: Easy to add new optional parameters
Very readable at the call site
cons: Risk of breaking changes if default values change
Can lead to confusion with many optional params

data.title: Exercise: Build a Calculator with Overloaded Methods
data.description: Create a Calculator class demonstrating method overloading, optional parameters, and return types.
steps: Create a new console project: `dotnet new console -n CalcMethods`
Create a `Calculator` class in the same file or a separate one
Add an overloaded `Add` method: one that takes 2 ints, one that takes 3 ints, and one that takes a `params int[]`
Add a `Divide` method that returns a double and handles division by zero
Add an optional parameter method `Power(double base, int exponent = 2)` that calculates base^exponent
Add an `out` parameter method `TryDivide(double a, double b, out double result)` that returns false if b is zero
In Program.cs, test all methods and print the results
data.expectedOutcome: A Calculator class with multiple overloaded Add methods, safe division, exponentiation, and TryDivide with out parameters — all tested in the main program.

items.question: When should I use a method vs inline code?
items.answer: Use a method when the logic is reused, complex, or needs a meaningful name. Inline code is fine for trivial one-off operations. Methods improve readability, enable reuse, and make testing easier.

items.question: What's the difference between ref and out?
items.answer: Both pass by reference, but `ref` requires the variable to be initialized before the call, and the method can read the initial value. `out` does not require initialization, but the method MUST assign a value before returning — it's designed for returning multiple values.

items.question: When should I use recursion?
items.answer: Recursion is ideal for problems with a natural recursive structure: tree traversal, factorial, Fibonacci, and divide-and-conquer algorithms. For simple iteration (like looping over a list), a `for` or `foreach` loop is clearer and more efficient.

items.question: Are local functions better than lambdas?
items.answer: Local functions are generally better when you need: generics, `ref`/`out` parameters, better stack traces, or a named function. Lambdas are better for short, inline delegates passed to methods like LINQ's `Where()`, `Select()`, etc.

items.question: Can I overload by return type alone?
items.answer: No. C# does not allow overloading methods based on return type alone. The parameter list must differ. For example, you cannot have `int GetValue()` and `string GetValue()` — the compiler cannot determine which to call based on return type.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Methods encapsulate reusable logic with parameters and return types
Use `void` for methods that don't return a value
Optional parameters use default values; named arguments improve readability
`params` allows a variable number of arguments
Method overloading provides flexibility with different parameter signatures
`ref` modifies caller's variable; `out` returns multiple values; `in` passes read-only by reference
Recursion solves problems by breaking them into smaller sub-problems
Local functions are scoped helpers defined inside another method
data.takeaway: Methods are the core of C# programming — mastering parameters, overloading, and reference semantics makes you a more effective developer.
